body.p: Blockciphers are the central tool in the design of protocols for shared-key (aka. symmetric) cryptography. They are the main available “technology” we have at our disposal. This chapter will take a look at these objects and describe the state of the art in their construction.

It is important to stress that blockciphers are just tools—raw ingredients for cooking up something more useful. Blockciphers don’t, by themselves, do something that an end-user would care about. As with any powerful tool, one has to learn to use this one. Even an excellent blockcipher won’t give you security if you don’t use it right. But used well, these are powerful tools indeed. Accordingly, an important theme in several upcoming chapters will be on how to use blockciphers well. We won’t be emphasizing how to design or analyze blockciphers, as this remains very much an art.

This chapter gets you acquainted with some typical blockciphers, and discusses attacks on them. In particular we’ll look at two examples, DES and AES. DES is the “old standby.” It is currently the most widely-used blockcipher in existence, and it is of sufficient historical significance that every trained cryptographer needs to have seen its description. AES is a modern blockcipher, and it is expected to supplant DES in the years to come.

sec.title: 3.1 What is a blockcipher?
sec.p: A blockcipher is a function E: {0,1}k × {0,1}n → {0,1}n. This notation means that E takes two inputs, one being a k-bit string and the other an n-bit string, and returns an n-bit string. The first input is the key. The second might be called the plaintext, and the output might be called a ciphertext. The key-length k and the block-length n are parameters associated to the blockcipher. They vary from blockcipher to blockcipher, as of course does the design of the algorithm itself.

For each key K ∈ {0,1}k we let EK: {0,1}n → {0,1}n be the function defined by EK(M) = E(K, M). For any blockcipher, and any key K, it is required that the function EK be a permutation on {0,1}n. This means that it is a bijection (i.e., a one-to-one and onto function) of {0,1}n to {0,1}n. (For every C ∈ {0,1}n there is exactly one M ∈ {0,1}n such that EK(M) = C.) Accordingly EK has an inverse, and we denote it EK−1. This function also maps {0,1}n to {0,1}n, and of course we have EK−1(EK(M)) = M and EK(EK−1(C)) = C for all M, C ∈ {0,1}n. We let E−1: {0,1}k × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be defined by E−1(K, C) = EK−1(C). This is the inverse blockcipher to E.

Preferably, the blockcipher E is a publicly specified algorithm. Both the cipher E and its inverse E−1 should be easily computable, meaning given K, M we can readily compute E(K, M), and given K, C we can readily compute E−1(K, C).

In typical usage, a random key K is chosen and kept secret between a pair of users. The function EK is then used by the two parties to process data in some way before they send it to each other. Typically, we will assume the adversary will be able to obtain some input-output examples for EK, meaning pairs of the form (M, C) where C = EK(M). But, ordinarily, the adversary will not be shown the key K. Security relies on the secrecy of the key. A blockcipher should be designed to make key recovery computationally difficult.

We emphasize that we’ve said absolutely nothing about what properties a blockcipher should have. A function like EK(M) = M is a blockcipher (the “identity blockcipher”), but we shall not regard it as a “good” one.

sec.title: 3.2 Data Encryption Standard (DES)
sec.p: The Data Encryption Standard (DES) is the quintessential blockcipher. Even though it is now quite old, and on the way out, no discussion of blockciphers can really omit mention of this construction. DES is a remarkably well-engineered algorithm which has had a powerful influence on cryptography. Every time you use an ATM machine, you are using DES.

sec.title: 3.2.1 A brief history
sec.p: In 1972 the NBS (National Bureau of Standards, now NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology) initiated a program for data protection and wanted as part of it an encryption algorithm that could be standardized. They put out a request for such an algorithm. In 1974, IBM responded with a design based on their “Lucifer” algorithm. This design would eventually evolve into the DES.
DES has a key-length of k = 56 bits and a block-length of n = 64 bits. It consists of 16 rounds of what is called a “Feistel network.” We will describe more details shortly.
After NBS, several other bodies adopted DES as a standard, including ANSI (the American National Standards Institute) and the American Bankers Association.

The standard was to be reviewed every five years to see whether or not it should be re-adopted. Although there were claims that it would not be re-certified, the algorithm was re-certified again and again. Only recently did the work for finding a replacement begin in earnest, in the form of the AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) effort.

sec.title: 3.2.2 Construction
sec.p: The DES algorithm is depicted in Fig. 3.1. It takes input a 56-bit key K and a 64-bit plaintext M. The key-schedule KeySchedule produces from the 56-bit key K a sequence of 16 subkeys, one for each of the rounds that follows. Each subkey is 48-bits long.

caption.p: The DES blockcipher. The text and other figures describe the subroutines KeySchedule, f, IP, IP−1.

disp-quote.p:
function DESK(M) // |K|=56 and |M|=64
(K1,...,K16) ← KeySchedule(K) // |Ki|=48 for 1≤i≤16
M ← IP(M)
Parse M as L0 ‖ R0 // |L0|=|R0|=32
for r = 1 to 16 do
Lr ← Rr−1; Rr ← f(Kr, Rr−1) ⊕ Lr−1
C ← IP−1(L16 ‖ R16)
return C

sec.p: The initial permutation IP simply permutes the bits of M, as described by the table of Fig. 3.2. The key is not involved in this permutation. The initial permutation does not appear to affect the cryptographic strength of the algorithm.

caption.p: Tables describing the DES initial permutation IP and its inverse IP−1.

sec.p: The permuted plaintext is now input to a loop, which operates on it in 16 rounds. Each round takes a 64-bit input, viewed as consisting of a 32-bit left half and a 32-bit right half, and, under the influence of the sub-key Kr, produces a 64-bit output. The input to round r is Lr−1 ‖ Rr−1, and the output of round r is Lr ‖ Rr. Each round is what is called a Feistel round, named after Horst Feistel, one of the IBM designers of a precursor of DES.

One of the reasons to use this round structure is that it is reversible, important to ensure that DES is a permutation for each key K. Indeed, given Lr ‖ Rr (and Kr) we can recover Lr−1 ‖ Rr−1 via Rr−1 ← Lr and Lr−1 ← f(Kr, Lr) ⊕ Rr.
Following the 16 rounds, the inverse of the permutation IP is applied to the 64-bit output of the 16th round, and the result is the output ciphertext.

A sequence of Feistel rounds is a common high-level design for a blockcipher. For a closer look we need to see how the function f(·,·) works. It is shown in Fig. 3.3. It takes a 48-bit subkey J and a 32-bit input R to return a 32-bit output. The 32-bit R is first expanded into a 48-bit value via the expansion function E described by the table of Fig. 3.4. Then the sub-key J is XORed with the output of E to yield a 48-bit result that is split into 8 blocks, each 6-bits long. To the i-th block we apply the function Si called the i-th S-box. Each S-box is a function taking 6 bits and returning 4 bits. The result is that the 48-bit value is compressed to 32 bits. These 32 bits are permuted according to the P permutation described in the table of Fig. 3.4, and the result is the output of the f function.

disp-quote.p:
function f(J, R) // |J|=48 and |R|=32
R ← E(R); R ← R ⊕ J
Parse R as R1 ‖ R2 ‖ R3 ‖ R4 ‖ R5 ‖ R6 ‖ R7 ‖ R8 // |Ri|=6 for 1≤i≤8
for i = 1,...,8 do
Ri ← Si(Ri) // Each S-box returns 4 bits
R ← R1 ‖ R2 ‖ R3 ‖ R4 ‖ R5 ‖ R6 ‖ R7 ‖ R8 // |R|=32 bits
R ← P(R)
return R

caption.p: Tables describing the expansion function E and final permutation P of the DES f-function.

sec.p: Each S-box is described by a table as shown in Fig. 3.5. Si takes a 6-bit input b1b2b3b4b5b6. Read b3b4b5b6 as a column index (0 to 15) and b1b2 as a row index. The table entry at that row and column gives the 4-bit output.
The S-boxes are the heart of the algorithm, and much effort was put into designing them to achieve various security goals and resistance to certain attacks.

caption.p: The DES S-boxes S1 through S8.

sec.p: Finally, the key schedule is shown in Fig. 3.6. Each round sub-key Kr is formed by taking some 48 bits of K. A permutation called PC-1 is first applied to the 56-bit key to yield a permuted version of it, divided into two 28-bit halves C0 ‖ D0. The algorithm goes through 16 rounds. The r-th round computes Cr ‖ Dr and applies a function PC-2 that extracts 48 bits from this 56-bit quantity. This is the sub-key Kr. The bits of Cr−1 are rotated to the left j positions to get Cr, and Dr is obtained similarly from Dr−1, where j is either 1 or 2, depending on r.

disp-quote.p:
Algorithm KeySchedule(K) // |K|=56
K ← PC-1(K)
Parse K as C0 ‖ D0
for r = 1,...,16 do
if r ∈ {1,2,9,16} then j ← 1 else j ← 2 fi
Cr ← leftshiftj(Cr−1); Dr ← leftshiftj(Dr−1)
Kr ← PC-2(Cr ‖ Dr)
return (K1,...,K16)

caption.p: Tables describing the PC-1 and PC-2 functions used by the DES key schedule of Fig. 3.6.

sec.p: Well now you know how DES works. Of course, the main questions about the design are: why, why and why? What motivated these design choices? We don’t know too much about this, although one of the designers of DES, Don Coppersmith, has written a short paper which provides some information.

sec.title: 3.2.3 Speed
sec.p: One of the design goals of DES was that it would have fast implementations relative to the technology of its time. In roughly current technology one can get well over 1 Gbit/sec on high-end VLSI. Specifically at least 1.6 Gbits/sec, maybe more. Perhaps a more interesting figure is that one can implement each DES S-box with at most 50 two-input gates, where the circuit has depth of only 3. Thus one can compute DES by a combinatorial circuit of about 8 · 16 · 50 = 640 gates and depth of 3 · 16 = 48 gates.

In software, on a fairly modern processor, DES takes something like 80 cycles per byte. This is disappointingly slow—not surprisingly, since DES was optimized for hardware and was designed before the days in which software implementations were considered feasible or desirable.

sec.title: 3.3 Key recovery attacks on blockciphers
sec.p: Now that we know what a blockcipher looks like, let us consider attacking one. This is called cryptanalysis of the blockcipher.

We fix a blockcipher E: {0,1}k × {0,1}n → {0,1}n having key-size k and block size n. Historically, cryptanalysis of blockciphers has focused on key-recovery. A k-bit key T, called the target key, is chosen at random. Given a sequence of q input-output examples of ET, the adversary wants to find T.

We say that a key K is consistent with the input-output examples (M1, C1), ..., (Mq, Cq) if EK(Mi) = Ci for all 1 ≤ i ≤ q. We let ConsE((M1, C1), ..., (Mq, Cq)) be the set of all keys consistent with the input-output examples.
Some typical kinds of attack:
Known-message attack: M1, ..., Mq are any distinct points; the adversary has no control over them.
Chosen-message attack: M1, ..., Mq are chosen by the adversary, perhaps even adaptively, via oracle access to the function EK.

The most obvious attack strategy is exhaustive key search. The adversary goes through all possible keys K′ ∈ {0,1}k until it finds one that explains the input-output pairs. The expected running time of this attack is approximately 2k−1 computations of the blockcipher. For DES (k = 56), using a VLSI chip at 1.6 Gbits/sec with a 64-bit block, this would take about 45.7 years. It turns out that DES has a property called key-complementation that reduces the search space by half, bringing this down to about 22.8 years.

Yet, the conclusion that DES is secure against exhaustive key search is actually too hasty. In 1993, Weiner argued that one can design a $1 million machine that does the exhaustive key search for DES in about 3.5 hours on the average. More recently, a DES key search machine was actually built by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, at a cost of $250,000, finding a key in 56 hours on average.

For DES, differential cryptanalysis is capable of finding a DES key using about 247 input-output examples in a chosen-message attack. Linear cryptanalysis improved this, requiring 244 known messages. However, the practical impact of these attacks is small, because obtaining 244 input-output examples and storing them is not feasible. So the best practical attack against DES is exhaustive key search.

DES is feeling its age. Yet it would be a mistake to take away the impression that DES is a weak algorithm. After all these years, the best practical attack known is still exhaustive key search. That says a lot for its design and its designers.

sec.title: 3.4 Iterated-DES and DESX
sec.p: The emergence of key-search engines led to the view that in practice DES should be considered broken. Its shortcoming was its key-length of 56, not long enough to resist exhaustive key search.

sec.title: 3.4.1 Double-DES
sec.p: Let K1, K2 be 56-bit DES keys and let M be a 64-bit plaintext. Let
This defines a blockcipher 2DES: {0,1}112 × {0,1}64 → {0,1}64 that we call Double-DES. It has a 112-bit key.
However, although 2DES has a key-length of 112, it turns out that it can be broken using about 257 DES and DES−1 computations by what is called a meet-in-the-middle attack. The observation is that:

disp-quote.p: C1 = DES(K2, DES(K1, M1)) ⇒ DES−1(K2, C1) = DES(K1, M1).

sec.p: This leads the attacker to: compute DES(Ti, M1) for all i = 1,...,256; compute DES−1(Tj, C1) for all j = 1,...,256; then find pairs (i, j) where the two lists collide. The total cost is 256 + 256 = 257 computations. The meet-in-the-middle attack shows that 2DES has an effective key length of only 57.
This attack is not particularly practical, because storing the two arrays of 256 entries each requires about 1.15 × 106 terabytes of storage.

sec.title: 3.4.2 Triple-DES
sec.p: The triple-DES ciphers use three iterations of DES or DES−1. The three-key variant is defined by

disp-quote.p: 3DES3(K1 ‖ K2 ‖ K3, M) = DES(K3, DES−1(K2, DES(K1, M)))

sec.p: so that 3DES3: {0,1}168 × {0,1}64 → {0,1}64. The two-key variant is defined by

disp-quote.p: 3DES2(K1 ‖ K2, M) = DES(K2, DES−1(K1, DES(K2, M)))

sec.p: so that 3DES2: {0,1}112 × {0,1}64 → {0,1}64. The rationale for the middle application being DES−1 rather than DES is that DES is easily recovered via DES(K, M) = 3DES3(K ‖ K ‖ K, M) and DES(K, M) = 3DES2(K ‖ K, M).

3DES3 is subject to a meet-in-the-middle attack using about 2112 computations, giving it an effective key length of 112. 3DES2 does not appear to be subject to such an attack, so its key length of 112 is also its effective key length. 3DES2 is popular in practice as a canonical replacement for DES.

sec.title: 3.4.3 DESX
sec.p: Although 2DES, 3DES3, and 3DES2 appear to provide adequate security, they are slow. A simple and much cheaper design is DESX. Let K be a 56-bit DES key, let K1, K2 be 64-bit strings, and let M be a 64-bit plaintext. Let

disp-quote.p: DESX(K1 ‖ K ‖ K2, M) = K2 ⊕ DES(K, K1 ⊕ M).

sec.p: This defines a blockcipher DESX: {0,1}184 × {0,1}64 → {0,1}64. Its 184-bit key precludes exhaustive key search attacks. A meet-in-the-middle attack finds the key using 2120 DES computations, so the effective key length of DESX is 120. DESX is popular because it is much cheaper than Double or Triple DES while providing adequate security.

sec.title: 3.4.4 Why a new cipher?
sec.p: DESX is arguably a fine cipher. Nonetheless, there were important reasons to find and standardize a new cipher. We will see later that the security provided by a blockcipher depends not only on its key length but on its block length. A blockcipher with block length n can be “broken” in time around 2n/2. When n = 64, this is 232, which is quite small. 2DES, 3DES3, 3DES2, and DESX all preserve the 64-bit block size of DES and are thus no more secure than DES from this point of view. A larger block length was one motivation for a new cipher. Perhaps the larger motivation was speed: a blockcipher that ran faster than DES in software was desired.

sec.title: 3.5 Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
sec.p: In 1998 the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST/USA) announced a “competition” for a new blockcipher. The relatively short key length of DES was the main problem that motivated the effort. Fifteen algorithms were submitted to NIST from around the world. In the summer of 2001 NIST announced their choice: an algorithm called Rijndael, designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen from Belgium.

The AES has a block length of n = 128 bits, and a key length k that is variable: it may be 128, 192 or 256 bits. So the standard actually specifies three different blockciphers: AES128, AES192, AES256. For simplicity we stick to describing AES128, writing C = AESK(M) where |K| = 128 and |M| = |C| = 128.

The high-level structure of AES is given in Fig. 3.8. The value s is called the state. AES consists of ten rounds. The rounds are identical except that each uses a different subkey Ki and, also, round 10 omits the call to mix-cols.

caption.p: The function AES128. See the accompanying text and figures for definitions of the maps expand, S, shift-rows, mix-cols.

disp-quote.p:
function AESK(M)
(K0,...,K10) ← expand(K)
s ← M ⊕ K0
for r = 1 to 10 do
s ← S(s)
s ← shift-rows(s)
if r ≤ 9 then s ← mix-cols(s) fi
s ← s ⊕ Kr
endfor
return s

sec.p: To understand what goes on in S and mix-cols we need to review a bit of algebra. We describe a way to do arithmetic on bytes. Identify each byte a = a7a6 ...a0 with the formal polynomial a7x7 + a6x6 + ... + a0. We can add two bytes by taking their bitwise XOR. We can multiply two bytes to get a polynomial, and then take the remainder modulo the fixed irreducible polynomial m(x) = x8 + x4 + x3 + x + 1. This yields the finite field GF(28).

The mapping S: {0,1}8 → {0,1}8 is obtained from the multiplicative inverse map inv: a ↦ a−1 in GF(28), patched so that inv({00}) = {00}, followed by an affine transformation. The resulting S-box is fully specified by Fig. 3.9.

caption.p: The AES S-box, which is a function S: {0,1}8 → {0,1}8. All values in hexadecimal. The meaning is: S(00) = 63, S(01) = 7c, ..., S(ff) = 16.

sec.p: The shift-rows operation imagines the 16 bytes of s plastered top-to-bottom, then left-to-right, into a 4×4 table. It then left circularly shifts the second row by one position; the third row by two positions; and the fourth row by three positions. The first row is not shifted at all.

The mix-cols step takes each of the four columns in the 4×4 table and applies the same transformation to it—matrix multiplication in GF(28) by the matrix with coefficients 02, 03, 01, 01 (cyclically), or equivalently, multiplication of the column as a polynomial by c(x) = {03}x3 + {01}x2 + {01}x + {02} modulo x4 + 1.

The key-expansion map expand is given in Fig. 3.10. One key property is that AES is a blockcipher: the map is invertible. This follows because every round is invertible, which in turn follows from each of its steps being invertible.

caption.p: The AES128 key-expansion algorithm maps a 128-bit key K into eleven 128-bit subkeys K0,...,K10.

disp-quote.p:
function expand(K)
K0 ← K
for i ← 1 to 10 do
Ki[0] ← Ki−1[0] ⊕ S(Ki−1[3] <<< 8) ⊕ Ci
Ki[1] ← Ki−1[1] ⊕ Ki[0]
Ki[2] ← Ki−1[2] ⊕ Ki[1]
Ki[3] ← Ki−1[3] ⊕ Ki[2]
od
return (K0,...,K10)

sec.p: In the case of DES, the rationale for the design was not made public. In the case of AES there was significantly more documentation of the rationale for design choices. Nonetheless, the security of blockciphers, including DES and AES, eventually comes down to the statement that “we have been unable to find effective attacks, and we have tried attacks along the following lines ....”

sec.title: 3.6 Limitations of key-recovery based security
sec.p: As discussed above, classically, the security of blockciphers has been looked at with regard to key recovery. A blockcipher is viewed as “secure” if the best key-recovery attack is computationally infeasible. In the sequel, we refer to this as security against key-recovery.

However, as a notion of security, security against key-recovery is quite limited. Even a cursory glance at common blockcipher usages shows that good security in the sense of key recovery is not sufficient for security of the usages of blockciphers.

As an example, consider the blockcipher E: {0,1}128 × {0,1}256 → {0,1}256 defined by EK(M) = AESK(M[1]) ‖ M[2] where M[1] is the first 128 bits of M and M[2] is the last 128 bits of M. Key recovery is as hard as for AES, but a ciphertext reveals the second half of the plaintext.

We need a single “master” property of a blockcipher which, if met, guarantees security of lots of natural usages of the cipher. Such a property is that the blockcipher be a pseudorandom permutation (PRP), a notion explored in another chapter.

sec.title: 3.7 Problems
sec.p: Problem 3.1 Show that for all K ∈ {0,1}56 and all x ∈ {0,1}64, DESK̅(x̅) = DESK(x). This is called the key-complementation property of DES.
Problem 3.2 Explain how to use the key-complementation property of DES to speed up exhaustive key search by about a factor of two. Explain any assumptions that you make.
Problem 3.3 Find a key K such that DESK(·) = DESK−1(·). Such a key is sometimes called a “weak” key.

Problem 3.4 As with AES, suppose we are working in the finite field with 28 elements, representing field points using the irreducible polynomial m(x) = x8 + x4 + x3 + x + 1. Compute the byte that is the result of multiplying bytes: {e1} · {05}.

Problem 3.5 For AES, we have given two different descriptions of mix-cols: one using matrix multiplication (in GF(28)) and one based on multiplying by a fixed polynomial c(x) modulo a second fixed polynomial d(x) = x4 + 1. Show that these two methods are equivalent.

Problem 3.6 Verify that the matrix used for mix-cols has as its inverse the matrix with rows (0e, 0b, 0d, 09), (09, 0e, 0b, 0d), (0d, 09, 0e, 0b), (0b, 0d, 09, 0e). Explain why all entries in this matrix begin with a zero.
Problem 3.7 How many different permutations are there from 128 bits to 128 bits? How many different functions are there from 128 bits to 128 bits?
Problem 3.8 Upper and lower bound, as best you can, the probability that a random function from 128 bits to 128 bits is actually a permutation.

Problem 3.9 Without consulting any of the numerous public-domain implementations available, implement AES, on your own, from the spec or from the description provided by this chapter. Then test your implementation according to the test vectors provided in the AES documentation.
Problem 3.10 Justify and then refute the following proposition: enciphering under AES can be implemented faster than deciphering.

Problem 3.11 Choose a random DES key K ∈ {0,1}56. Let (M, C), where C = DESK(M), be a single plaintext/ciphertext pair that an adversary knows. Suppose the adversary does an exhaustive key search to locate the lexicographically first key T such that C = DEST(M). Estimate the probability that T = K. Discuss any assumptions you must make to answer this question.
